claim: Two-thirds of gene promoters in mammals are associated with regions of non-methylated DNA, called CpG islands (CGIs).
source: Two-thirds of gene promoters in mammals are associated with regions of non-methylated DNA, called CpG islands (CGIs), which counteract the repressive effects of DNA methylation on chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about mammalian gene promoters.

claim: CpG islands counteract the repressive effects of DNA methylation on chromatin.
source: Two-thirds of gene promoters in mammals are associated with regions of non-methylated DNA, called CpG islands (CGIs), which counteract the repressive effects of DNA methylation on chromatin.
evidence: This is stated as a functional property of CGIs in the abstract.

claim: In cold-blooded vertebrates, computational CGI predictions often reside away from gene promoters.
source: In cold-blooded vertebrates, computational CGI predictions often reside away from gene promoters, suggesting a major divergence in gene promoter architecture across vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a prior observation from computational predictions.

claim: Non-methylated islands (NMIs) of DNA are a central feature of vertebrate gene promoters.
source: By experimentally identifying non-methylated DNA in the genomes of seven diverse vertebrates, we instead reveal that non-methylated islands (NMIs) of DNA are a central feature of vertebrate gene promoters.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data from seven vertebrate species.

claim: NMIs are present at orthologous genes across vast evolutionary distances.
source: Furthermore, NMIs are present at orthologous genes across vast evolutionary distances, revealing a surprising level of conservation in this epigenetic feature.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by comparative analysis across species.

claim: Short contiguous regions of non-methylated DNA are found associated with most human and mouse gene promoters.
source: Short contiguous regions of non-methylated DNA are found associated with most human and mouse gene promoters, where they create a transcriptionally permissive chromatin environment (Blackledge et al., 2010; Thomson et al., 2010; Blackledge and Klose, 2011; Deaton and Bird, 2011; Jones, 2012) that opposes the repressive effects of DNA methylation (Klose and Bird, 2006; Weber and Schubeler, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Non-methylated regions create a transcriptionally permissive chromatin environment.
source: Short contiguous regions of non-methylated DNA are found associated with most human and mouse gene promoters, where they create a transcriptionally permissive chromatin environment (Blackledge et al., 2010; Thomson et al., 2010; Blackledge and Klose, 2011; Deaton and Bird, 2011; Jones, 2012) that opposes the repressive effects of DNA methylation (Klose and Bird, 2006; Weber and Schubeler, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In non-methylated regions, CpG dinucleotide frequency is elevated compared to surrounding sequence.
source: In non-methylated regions, CpG dinucleotide frequency is elevated compared to surrounding sequence (Bird et al., 1985; Bird, 1987).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Accelerated methyl-cytosine mutability leads to a reduction in CpG dinucleotide frequency in densely methylated regions of the genome over evolutionary time.
source: This is due to accelerated methyl-cytosine mutability, which over evolutionary time leads to a reduction in CpG dinucleotide frequency in densely methylated regions of the genome, while CpG frequency is preserved in non-methylated regions (Coulondre et al., 1978; Bird, 1980).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations explaining the mechanism.

claim: CpG frequency is preserved in non-methylated regions over evolutionary time.
source: This is due to accelerated methyl-cytosine mutability, which over evolutionary time leads to a reduction in CpG dinucleotide frequency in densely methylated regions of the genome, while CpG frequency is preserved in non-methylated regions (Coulondre et al., 1978; Bird, 1980).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Algorithms were developed to predict non-methylated regions of DNA based primarily on elevated local G+C content and CpG dinucleotide frequency.
source: Taking advantage of the methylation-dependent variations in nucleotide frequency observed in mammals, algorithms were developed to predict non-methylated regions of DNA based primarily on elevated local G+C content and CpG dinucleotide frequency (Gardiner-Garden and Frommer, 1987; Takai and Jones, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In mouse and human roughly 50–65% of transcription start sites (TSSs) overlap with CGI predictions.
source: In mouse and human roughly 50–65% of transcription starts sites (TSSs) overlap with CGI predictions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a known observation.

claim: Only 16% of zebrafish TSSs overlap predicted CGIs.
source: Interestingly, CGI predictions in cold-blooded vertebrates often reside away from gene promoters, with only 16% of zebrafish and 17% of frog TSSs overlapping predicted CGIs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a prior observation from computational predictions.

claim: Only 17% of frog TSSs overlap predicted CGIs.
source: Interestingly, CGI predictions in cold-blooded vertebrates often reside away from gene promoters, with only 16% of zebrafish and 17% of frog TSSs overlapping predicted CGIs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a prior observation from computational predictions.

claim: Non-methylated DNA has been suggested to be a unique feature of gene promoters in endotherms.
source: This has led to the suggestion that non-methylated DNA is a unique feature of gene promoters in endotherms, potentially representing a major divergence in the usage of this epigenetic system between warm-blooded and cold-blooded vertebrates (Aïssani and Bernardi, 1991; Sharif et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a prior hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: CGI prediction does not accurately identify islands of non-methylated DNA, particularly in lower vertebrates.
source: Interestingly we reveal that CGI prediction does not accurately identify islands of non-methylated DNA, particularly in lower vertebrates.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction, supported by experimental data comparing CGI predictions to experimentally identified NMIs.

claim: The distribution of experimentally identified NMIs was strikingly similar across all seven species.
source: In these regions, the location of computationally derived CGIs in relation to orthologous genes differs greatly across the seven species. In contrast, the distribution of our experimentally identified NMIs was strikingly similar across all seven species.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by visual evidence in Figure 1A.

claim: In human, roughly 50-60% of experimental NMIs lay outside of predicted CGIs.
source: In human, mouse and chicken, NMIs encompassed most CGI predictions, although in human and mouse roughly 50–60% of experimental NMIs lay outside of predicted CGIs in agreement with recent genome-wide bisulfite sequencing studies (Molaro et al., 2011; Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: In mouse, roughly 50-60% of experimental NMIs lay outside of predicted CGIs.
source: In human, mouse and chicken, NMIs encompassed most CGI predictions, although in human and mouse roughly 50–60% of experimental NMIs lay outside of predicted CGIs in agreement with recent genome-wide bisulfite sequencing studies (Molaro et al., 2011; Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The overlap between NMIs and predicted CGIs in lower vertebrates was surprisingly poor.
source: Interestingly, the overlap between NMIs and predicted CGIs in lower vertebrates was surprisingly poor revealing that CGI maps in most species fail to accurately identify regions of non-methylated DNA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: Human and mouse NMIs show elevated CpG O/E and GC content compared to control regions of the genome.
source: As expected, human and mouse NMIs show elevated CpG O/E and GC content compared to control regions of the genome (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Many human and mouse NMIs have lower CpG O/E and GC content than the CGI predictions.
source: However, many human and mouse NMIs have lower CpG O/E and GC content than the CGI predictions, explaining why the CGI predictions do not accurately identify all NMIs in these species.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: NMIs in chicken have the highest CpG O/E and GC content compared to the surrounding genome amongst all the vertebrates examined.
source: This appears to be due to the fact that NMIs in this species have the highest CpG O/E and GC content compared to the surrounding genome amongst all the vertebrates examined.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: Platypus genome is on average more CpG and GC rich than chicken.
source: Although platypus NMIs have a similarly high CpG O/E and GC content, its genome is on average more CpG and GC rich than chicken.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: The high CpG and GC richness of the platypus genome causes the algorithm to massively over-predict CGIs.
source: Although platypus NMIs have a similarly high CpG O/E and GC content, its genome is on average more CpG and GC rich than chicken. This causes the algorithm to massively over-predict CGIs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Lizard and frog encode NMIs with CpG O/E content similar to those in mammals, but with lower GC content.
source: Lizard and frog encode NMIs with CpG O/E content similar to those in mammals, but with lower GC content.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: In zebrafish, NMI CpG O/E is high yet the GC content is almost indistinguishable from surrounding DNA sequence.
source: In zebrafish, NMI CpG O/E is high yet the GC content is almost indistinguishable from surrounding DNA sequence (Cross et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and data in Figure 1C.

claim: The failure of CpG island prediction algorithms to accurately identify NMIs in different species is dependent on the variation in CpG density and G+C content amongst vertebrate genomes.
source: The failure of CpG island prediction algorithms to accurately identify NMIs in different species is almost certainly dependent on the variation in CpG density and G+C content amongst vertebrate genomes, but also will rely on genome assembly and annotation quality, particularly of repetitive elements.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Species differences in nucleotide content are likely driven by the relative strengths of two processes: reductions of G+C content due to imperfect repair of spontaneous 5-methylcytosine deamination events and increases in G+C content in species and genomic regions that are especially prone to GC-biased gene conversion.
source: These sequence variations between species are likely driven by the relative strengths of two processes: reductions of G+C content due to imperfect repair of spontaneous 5-methylcytosine deamination events (Coulondre et al., 1978; Bird, 1980) and increases in G+C content in species and genomic regions that are especially prone to GC-biased gene conversion, an outcome of recombination (Duret and Galtier, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Non-methylated DNA fragments, even with low CpG density, are effectively detected by Bio-CAP.
source: In contrast, non-methylated DNA fragments, even with low CpG density, are effectively detected by Bio-CAP (Blackledge et al., 2012) and a broad distribution of CpG density within NMIs is identified in all species.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: 72% of human TSSs of protein coding genes overlap with an NMI.
source: In human, mouse, and chicken we observed that most TSSs of protein coding genes overlap with an NMI (72%, 66%, 58%, respectively) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: 66% of mouse TSSs of protein coding genes overlap with an NMI.
source: In human, mouse, and chicken we observed that most TSSs of protein coding genes overlap with an NMI (72%, 66%, 58%, respectively) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: 58% of chicken TSSs of protein coding genes overlap with an NMI.
source: In human, mouse, and chicken we observed that most TSSs of protein coding genes overlap with an NMI (72%, 66%, 58%, respectively) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: 55% of zebrafish TSSs overlap with NMIs.
source: In stark contrast, our new NMI maps reveal strong overlap of NMIs and TSSs (55%) in zebrafish.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Using RNA-seq information to refine TSS annotation increased the fraction of TSSs overlapping NMIs in lizard and frog to 45–58%.
source: However, by using RNA-seq information to refine TSS annotation (Akkers et al., 2010; Barbosa-Morais et al., 2012), the fraction of TSSs overlapping NMIs in these species increased to 45–58%, similar to that observed in other vertebrates (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations and data in Figure 2A.

claim: Non-methylated DNA signal centres at TSSs in all seven species.
source: Nevertheless, non-methylated DNA signal centres at TSSs in all seven species (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Over 90% of NMIs are shared at orthologous gene TSSs between human and each of the other six species examined.
source: This is exemplified by the fact that over 90% of NMIs are shared at orthologous gene TSSs between human and each of the other six species examined.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: Nearly all gene promoters of one-to-one orthologues between human, mouse and zebrafish have conserved NMIs, despite 450 million years of divergent evolution.
source: Furthermore, a more extensive three-way comparison between human, mouse and zebrafish revealed conservation of NMIs at nearly all gene promoters of one-to-one orthologues, despite 450 million years of divergent evolution (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: An unexpectedly large proportion of vertebrate NMIs lie within intergenic regions.
source: In addition to gene associated NMIs, an unexpectedly large proportion of vertebrate NMIs lie within intergenic regions (Figure 4A), suggesting that some NMIs may be functioning in regulatory roles away from known gene promoters.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: Histone H3 lysine 4 mono-methylation (H3K4me1) has been found to be strongly associated with enhancer elements.
source: Recently, histone H3 lysine 4 mono-methylation (H3K4me1) has been found to be strongly associated with enhancer elements (Barski et al., 2007; Heintzman et al., 2007; Aday et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: In mouse and zebrafish 45–64% of known lncRNA TSSs were associated with NMIs.
source: However, in mouse and zebrafish 45–64% of known lncRNA TSSs (Guttman et al., 2010; Belgard et al., 2011; Ulitsky et al., 2011; Pauli et al., 2012) were associated with NMIs suggesting that this class of candidate regulatory RNAs are subject to similar epigenetic regulatory processes as protein coding genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations and data in Figure 4B.

claim: Association with the TSSs of all known non-coding transcripts accounted for 15% and 9% of intergenic NMIs in mouse and zebrafish respectively.
source: In total, association with the TSSs of all known non-coding transcripts accounted for 15% and 9% of intergenic NMIs in mouse and zebrafish respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: 17% and 40% of intergenic NMIs in mouse and zebrafish respectively corresponded to putative enhancers.
source: Intergenic NMIs not associated with annotated non-coding RNAs were then compared with H3K4me1 peaks and a further 17% and 40% of the NMIs, in mouse and zebrafish respectively, corresponded to putative enhancers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Up to 14% and 8% of NMIs in mouse and zebrafish overlap with uncharacterised transcribed regions of the genome.
source: Finally, the remaining intergenic NMIs were compared to tissue-specific RNA-seq datasets (Stadler et al., 2011) to determine whether they overlapped with un-annotated transcriptional initiation. This revealed that up to 14% and 8% of NMIs in mouse and zebrafish overlap with uncharacterised transcribed regions of the genome.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and data in Figure 4C.

claim: 46–57% of NMIs away from the 5′ end of protein coding genes encompass known ncRNA TSSs, putative enhancers, and other transcribed regions.
source: Therefore a substantial proportion (46–57%) of NMIs away from the 5′ end of protein coding genes encompass known ncRNA TSSs, putative enhancers, and other transcribed regions, a property which is highly conserved across two diverse vertebrate species.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the data.

claim: NMIs in mammals are thought to be maintained in the non-methylated state in most tissues, even if their associated gene is not appreciably transcribed.
source: In general NMIs in mammals are thought to be maintained in the non-methylated state in most tissues, even if their associated gene is not appreciably transcribed.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a general belief.

claim: Some NMIs in human and mouse are susceptible to differential methylation during tissue specification.
source: Recently this belief has been challenged and it appears that some NMIs in human and mouse are more susceptible to differential methylation during tissue specification (Weber et al., 2007; Farthing et al., 2008; Mohn et al., 2008; Straussman et al., 2009; Illingworth et al., 2010; Maunakea et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: All vertebrates utilise differential methylation to epigenetically regulate a subset of NMIs.
source: The existence of unique NMIs in each of the interrogated tissues suggests that all vertebrates utilise differential methylation to epigenetically regulate a subset of NMIs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Shared NMIs tended to be longer and have higher CpG density.
source: Interestingly, it was immediately apparent that shared and unique NMIs stratified into two largely distinct classes. Shared NMIs tended to be longer, have higher CpG density (Figure 5C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D) and are generally found associated with the TSSs of protein coding genes (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Shared NMIs are generally found associated with the TSSs of protein coding genes.
source: Interestingly, it was immediately apparent that shared and unique NMIs stratified into two largely distinct classes. Shared NMIs tended to be longer, have higher CpG density (Figure 5C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D) and are generally found associated with the TSSs of protein coding genes (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: Tissue-specific NMIs that are differentially methylated tended to be shorter, have lower CpG density and are found away from protein-coding gene TSSs.
source: In contrast, tissue-specific NMIs that are differentially methylated tended to be shorter, have lower CpG density and are found away from protein-coding gene TSSs (Figure 5B–D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Genes differentially expressed between liver and testes were significantly enriched for genes with tissue-specific NMIs.
source: This revealed that genes differentially expressed between liver and testes were significantly enriched for genes with tissue-specific NMIs (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The presence of DNA methylation closely correlates with gene repression.
source: Therefore, the presence of DNA methylation closely correlates with gene repression, suggesting that although an infrequent event, methylation-mediated silencing at NMI promoters is a general feature in epigenetic regulation of certain vertebrate protein-coding genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Methylation-mediated silencing at NMI promoters is a general feature in epigenetic regulation of certain vertebrate protein-coding genes.
source: Therefore, the presence of DNA methylation closely correlates with gene repression, suggesting that although an infrequent event, methylation-mediated silencing at NMI promoters is a general feature in epigenetic regulation of certain vertebrate protein-coding genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Most tissue-specific NMIs are intergenic.
source: Most tissue-specific NMIs are intergenic, indicating that differential methylation of these elements in vertebrate genomes is generally found away from known gene promoters (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: NMIs are recognized by a class of ZF-CxxC DNA binding proteins that recruit chromatin modifying enzymes to create a unique chromatin environment including placement of H3K4me3.
source: Recently, we and others have demonstrated that NMIs are recognized by a class of ZF-CxxC DNA binding proteins that recruit chromatin modifying enzymes to create a unique chromatin environment including placement of H3K4me3 (Blackledge et al., 2010; Thomson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: There was a very clear segregation of H3K4me3 with the tissue that has the unique NMI in human and mouse.
source: To examine whether differential methylation of NMIs corresponds to alterations in H3K4me3, the levels of this modification were examined in testes and liver in both human and mouse. This revealed a very clear segregation of H3K4me3 with the tissue that has the unique NMI (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: There was a clear enrichment of H3K4me3 at tissue-specific NMIs in frog and zebrafish.
source: Similarly, when we extended this analysis to the lower vertebrates frog and zebrafish there was a clear enrichment of H3K4me3 at tissue-specific NMIs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: Differential DNA methylation at gene promoters is associated with gene repression.
source: Together these observations demonstrate that differential DNA methylation at gene promoters is associated with gene repression and that the chromatin modification state of differentially methylated NMIs may be regulated in a switch-like mechanism dependent on the underlying DNA methylation status.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: The chromatin modification state of differentially methylated NMIs may be regulated in a switch-like mechanism dependent on the underlying DNA methylation status.
source: Together these observations demonstrate that differential DNA methylation at gene promoters is associated with gene repression and that the chromatin modification state of differentially methylated NMIs may be regulated in a switch-like mechanism dependent on the underlying DNA methylation status.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: A subset of genes are encompassed by broad regions of non-methylated DNA ('broad NMIs') that often cover the majority of the gene.
source: Interestingly however, we observed a subset of genes that deviated from this generality and tended to be encompassed by broad regions of non-methylated DNA ('broad NMIs') that often covered the majority of the gene.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 7A.

claim: Broad NMIs appear to be H3K4me3 modified over the entire non-methylated region.
source: Like canonical NMIs, broad NMIs appear to be H3K4me3 modified over the entire non-methylated region indicating they are also targeted by ZF-CxxC dependent chromatin modifying activities (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 7B,C.

claim: Genes encompassed by broad NMIs are highly enriched for transcription factors and genes involved in development.
source: Interestingly, genes encompassed by broad NMIs are highly enriched for transcription factors and genes involved in development, suggesting that this epigenetic feature may be related to the mechanisms that underpin their transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 7D.

claim: 45% of broad NMIs were associated with H3K27me3 in mouse ES cells.
source: Strikingly 45% and 89% of broad NMIs were associated with H3K27me3 in mouse ES cells and frog stage 11–12 tissues respectively, a significantly higher proportion than observed for canonical NMIs (Fisher's exact test, odds ratio > 5.3, p<10−35).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 7E.

claim: 89% of broad NMIs were associated with H3K27me3 in frog stage 11–12 tissues.
source: Strikingly 45% and 89% of broad NMIs were associated with H3K27me3 in mouse ES cells and frog stage 11–12 tissues respectively, a significantly higher proportion than observed for canonical NMIs (Fisher's exact test, odds ratio > 5.3, p<10−35).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 7E.

claim: H3K27me3 extends across the broad region of non-methylated DNA.
source: As with H3K4me3, H3K27me3 extends across the broad region of non-methylated DNA suggesting that not only are broad NMIs preferentially subject to polycomb silencing but that polycomb complexes may also read the underlying non-methylated DNA state when placing H3K27me3 marks (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 7F.

claim: Polycomb complexes may read the underlying non-methylated DNA state when placing H3K27me3 marks.
source: As with H3K4me3, H3K27me3 extends across the broad region of non-methylated DNA suggesting that not only are broad NMIs preferentially subject to polycomb silencing but that polycomb complexes may also read the underlying non-methylated DNA state when placing H3K27me3 marks (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a speculation based on the data.

claim: Broad NMIs specify a unique subset of transcription factors and developmental regulators that are preferentially targeted for polycomb repression during early development.
source: Together this demonstrates that broad NMIs specify a unique subset of transcription factors and developmental regulators that are preferentially targeted for polycomb repression during early development, a process that appears to be highly conserved over vertebrate evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: CGI maps had previously indicated that the DNA methylation system may have significantly diverged between vertebrate species.
source: Although the DNA methylation system is conserved across vertebrate evolution, CGI maps had previously indicated that this epigenetic system may have significantly diverged between vertebrate species and even acquired unique properties at TSSs during the evolution of warm-blooded vertebrates (Aïssani and Bernardi, 1991; Sharif et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Three distinct yet highly conserved classes of NMIs have emerged during vertebrate evolution.
source: Importantly, this paradigm shift also revealed that three distinct yet highly conserved classes of NMIs have emerged during vertebrate evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The first class is a canonical NMI that best fits the classical definition of a CGI.
source: The first class is a canonical NMI that best fits the classical definition of a CGI. These NMIs are narrow, associated with gene promoters, and generally remain free of DNA methylation regardless of the tissue or associated gene expression state.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Canonical NMIs are narrow, associated with gene promoters, and generally remain free of DNA methylation regardless of the tissue or associated gene expression state.
source: The first class is a canonical NMI that best fits the classical definition of a CGI. These NMIs are narrow, associated with gene promoters, and generally remain free of DNA methylation regardless of the tissue or associated gene expression state.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The second class of plastic NMIs are shorter, have lower CpG density than canonical NMIs, are usually found away from gene promoters at alternative regulatory elements, and are subject to differential methylation between tissues.
source: The second class of plastic NMIs are shorter, have lower CpG density than canonical NMIs, are usually found away from gene promoters at alternative regulatory elements, and are subject to differential methylation between tissues.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Epigenetic plasticity in the form of differential methylation is a highly conserved mechanism utilised by all vertebrates.
source: Importantly, this class of NMI demonstrates that epigenetic plasticity in the form of differential methylation is a highly conserved mechanism utilised by all vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: A third and unique class of broad NMIs often cover an entire gene, are specifically associated with transcription factors or developmental genes, and are associated with polycomb mediated silencing during early development.
source: Finally, a third and unique class of broad NMIs were identified that often cover an entire gene, are specifically associated with transcription factors or developmental genes, and are associated with polycomb mediated silencing during early development.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The central properties that underpin the NMI system are highly conserved across vertebrates.
source: Therefore, in contrast to the suggestion that NMIs may have diverged during vertebrate evolution (Aïssani and Bernardi, 1991; Sharif et al., 2010), we demonstrate that the central properties that underpin the NMI system are instead highly conserved across vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: TSS-associated NMIs appear to be under strong selective pressure as part of a highly conserved epigenetic system used to specify and control gene regulatory elements in large and complex vertebrate genomes.
source: Perhaps most importantly, TSS-associated NMIs appears to be under strong selective pressure as part of what appears to be a highly conserved epigenetic system used to specify and control gene regulatory elements in large and complex vertebrate genomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Bio-CAP was performed in duplicate with matched input controls.
source: All Bio-CAP experiments were performed in duplicate with matched input controls.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Next generation sequencing was performed using two Illumina sequencing platforms: Genome Analyser IIx and HiSeq Systems yielding 51-bp single-end reads.
source: Next generation sequencing was performed using two Illumina sequencing platforms: Genome Analyser IIx and HiSeq Systems yielding 51-bp single-end reads.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The location of computationally derived CGIs in relation to orthologous genes differs greatly across the seven species.
source: In these regions, the location of computationally derived CGIs in relation to orthologous genes differs greatly across the seven species.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by visual evidence in Figure 1A.

claim: In human, mouse and chicken, NMIs encompassed most CGI predictions.
source: In human, mouse and chicken, NMIs encompassed most CGI predictions, although in human and mouse roughly 50–60% of experimental NMIs lay outside of predicted CGIs in agreement with recent genome-wide bisulfite sequencing studies (Molaro et al., 2011; Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: CGI predictions in chicken are surprisingly accurate.
source: CGI predictions in chicken are surprisingly accurate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the data.

claim: The pairwise comparison of NMIs at orthologous gene TSSs was found to be highly statistically significant for all comparisons across the seven vertebrate species (p<10−10, hypergeometric test).
source: The percentage of NMIs conserved at orthologous gene TSSs was calculated in a pairwise manner and found to be highly statistically significant for all comparisons across the seven vertebrate species (p<10−10, hypergeometric test).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 3A caption.

claim: Less than 3% of intergenic NMIs overlapped with the primary transcripts of miRNAs, rRNAs, snRNAs, or snoRNAs.
source: Initially we analysed whether intergenic NMIs were found associated with the TSSs of annotated non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) and found that less than 3% overlapped with the primary transcripts of miRNAs, rRNAs, snRNAs, or snoRNAs (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Unique NMIs from liver or testes were validated by bisulfite sequencing for mouse and zebrafish.
source: Unique NMIs from liver or testes were validated by bisulfite sequencing for mouse and zebrafish (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mammalian NMI-associated TSSs are generally refractory to DNA methylation in most tissues.
source: This is consistent with the classical view that mammalian NMI-associated TSSs are generally refractory to DNA methylation in most tissues (Illingworth et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Genes with tissue-specific NMIs were significantly over-represented in the set of genes which had increased differential expression in seven out of eight cases.
